alanian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Don and Kuban rivers and northern Caucasian approaches funnel open pasture into fewer crossings. When grazing fails, neighboring permission determines where camps can move. Links from Uspe toward Black Sea markets also matter to grain. Steppe distance is measured not only by riders but by wagons, young animals and remounts. Rain changes crossings, while winter camps need shelter and forage; one usable entrance can matter to several families.

[Authority and government] Beler’s standing depends on protecting people and horses and delivering rewards. Courage wins followers, but lost household wagons and winter pasture diminish protection promises. Beler does not hold a register that directly commands everyone. Riders brought by each chief retain kin connections. Shared recognition strengthens assembly while requiring wagon guards and people left at home.

[Economy and livelihood] Alan households move with herds. Lost mounts, breeding females and household wagons affect the next season; silver buys goods but cannot instantly restore tired horses or breeding stock. Exchange brings grain, iron and leatherwork into camp. Alan movement also concerns how grain catches up with herds. Good pasture does not imply nearby food for exchange. Interrupted coastal contact may require smaller concentrations or separate trading parties and wagons, each adding escorts and coordination. An army’s ability to ride is therefore different from the ability of its supporting households to remain together.

[Forces and mobilization] Alan riders depend on mounts, remounts and grazing. Long weapons and riding skills still need rested horses; distant pursuit strains return routes, camp protection and food together. Once riders leave, opponents may bypass them to reach dependants.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] War with Huns and Bosporans threatens different approaches; Gothic and Caucasian cooperation can share warning duties. A Bosporan truce offers more than one fewer opponent: it can restore conversion of animals into food. Gothic or Caucasian protection for a road still requires numbers, duration and grazing terms. Personal friendship cannot solve carrying capacity, and a partner providing passage need not accept every dependant or every herd.

[Internal society] Alan chiefs maintain separate followings and pasture arrangements. Joint campaigning does not put every household under one camp. Consent over grazing, wagon protection and service reduces fragmentation. Beler must make movement avoid abandoning one family while resistance avoids the loss of everyone’s animals. Dispersed camps reduce the damage of one attack but complicate messages and relief. Concentration and dispersal thus have concrete costs, with neither providing safety automatically; the distribution of those costs affects continued allegiance.
alemannic_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Upper Rhine routes, former Roman borderland and woods toward the Danube give Segodunum connections and obstacles. Few crossings matter disproportionately, and neighboring war forces merchants into detours. The Rhine is both boundary and route, with cargo and armies using similar crossings. Woodland hides small parties but slows heavy loads; Segodunum’s connections cannot be understood as straight lines.

[Authority and government] Makrian gains recognition through martial success, oaths and participation. Roman agreements preserve markets only when local chiefs also implement them. Makrian’s summons becomes people and food through local chiefs.

[Economy and livelihood] Farming and livestock east of the upper Rhine connect through crossings with Roman coins, objects and markets. Closed borders hurt both elite gifts and household exchange; harvest and herds outlast one haul of prizes. The same settlement can support fighters and traders, with losses from a closed crossing entering arguments among chiefs.

[Forces and mobilization] Woods and Rhine crossings support warnings and ambush. Assembly removes farm labor; how long followers remain depends on food and return dates as well as commands. River watchers distinguish merchants, envoys and enemies. False alarms damage contact, missed warnings expose homes, and concentration at one crossing increases the need for messengers elsewhere.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Franks are the current enemy and Quadi friendly; envoys can still negotiate with Rome. Operations against Franks can alarm Rome and enlarge a local rivalry. Makrian’s diplomatic room depends on defined frontier aims and confidence that an oath will not leave other chiefs carrying food and crossing duties alone. Practical guarantees matter more than a claim that every participant has become permanently friendly.

[Internal society] Alamannic groups follow several chiefs. Makrian coordinates action while others retain families, followers and interests. Markets reward some groups while campaigning builds others’ reputation. Royal prestige does not absorb every other chief’s discretion. Participants retain reasons to resist excessive obligations. Prizes fund one action, whereas restored fields, herds and markets support the next assembly. Leadership must remain credible on both timescales, explaining why a negotiated pause can serve martial standing rather than simply undermine it.
angle_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Narrow southern peninsula routes meet bays and landing places. Inland roads supply food and water; conflict toward Saxons can threaten both land travel and landing. A blocked southern road changes maritime supply too, and coastal weather can delay even a short voyage.

[Authority and government] Protection includes home security and safe return. Gifts favoring a few families make other households question further men and vessels. Wihtlaeg needs to distinguish those supplying ships, grain or home guards. Owners and chiefs turn agreement into an actual force rather than an intention voiced at a feast.

[Economy and livelihood] Angulus households combine fields, livestock, fishing and coastal exchange. Vessels carry goods and people; requisition or delayed return reduces farm labor and winter stores. Land and sea routes draw on the same grain and repair resources. An easy landing cannot necessarily sustain every crew for long. Peninsula households calculate not only a voyage’s returns but who tends animals and carries the next food to shore while vessels and workers are absent. These arrangements shape the force available before sailing.

[Forces and mobilization] Coastal operations depend on tide, water, repair and landings. Land fighters also need food; sending every person aboard leaves fields and routes unguarded. Landing forces need boat guards while inland routes need warnings; the same skilled people cannot do both.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] The Saxon war threatens southern routes; Danish friendship helps retain strait connections. Limited Saxon operations, captive exchange and passage agreements turn competition into terms participants can deliver. Danish partners may assist voyages without assuming every southern dispute. Each arrangement therefore depends on the actual owners and chiefs attending, rather than an assumption that shared friendship commits all vessels at any time.

[Internal society] Wihtlaeg relies on kin chiefs and sailing partners. Crews, owners and cultivators bear different risks, requiring agreed numbers, shares and return dates. Wihtlaeg’s standing is vulnerable if it rests only on successful expeditions. Protection at home, timely return and recognition of different contributions keep support from those not carrying weapons. A reward matters through the real cost it offsets; visible care for suppliers can make another assembly possible after an inconclusive campaign.
antean_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Rivers and wetlands at the forest-steppe edge concentrate travel at crossings. Open ground admits cavalry while woodland branches retain escape routes. Sarum’s safety lies not only in settlement defences but in tracks to woods, banks and neighboring villages. Grain and dependants move slower than lightly equipped fighters, so late warning congests exits.

[Authority and government] Recognition comes from protecting villages and coordinating kin. A royal name cannot replace relief; returned captives and preserved harvests make protection visible. Bozh’s coalition needs local messengers and hosts, not an assumption of equal stores. Shared watch still leaves settlements responsible for household affairs.

[Economy and livelihood] Households around Sarum depend on valley farming, herds and woodland products. Grain feeds families and assembled fighters; blocked woodland exchange makes iron and imported salt harder to replace. Valley harvest entering a coalition does not become a store usable everywhere. Grain needs carriers and guards, while seed retained by households determines the next crop. Displacement separates stores from fields, making safe passage central to recovery rather than merely a military convenience. A force can hold ground without restoring the livelihoods that fed it.

[Forces and mobilization] Banks, woods and warnings help foot fighters avoid cavalry advantages. Pursuit lengthens supply and messages; people who know exits help fighters return.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Sarmatians are the current enemy; friendly Sclaveni and Venedians can negotiate passage. Sarmatian disputes can involve people, animals and exchangeable food together. Returned captives may strengthen recognition more than distant occupation. Friendly settlements offer mediation, but hosting outsiders adds ration pressure. Assistance must therefore specify what the host can provide rather than assume that kinship or goodwill removes the cost.

[Internal society] Bozh connects settlements and local leaders. Warnings require messengers and guards, and equal levies impose different costs on villages with different stores. Villages differ in exposure, reserves and relatives already lost. Their choices are more complex than willingness or fear of fighting. Bozh must show weaker communities that union brings protection rather than repeated early collection and late relief. How aid is distributed influences whether local leaders continue passing warnings and contributing people.
armenian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] The Araxes valley and highland passes lead toward Rome and Persia. Season, snow and provisioned sites determine routes for caravans and aid. Valley roads carry plain grain uphill, with snow and scarce pack animals reducing both merchants and aid. Holding a pass does not ensure food behind it; Duin and the Araxes links matter equally.

[Authority and government] Varazdat’s Arsacid position also needs aristocratic and church recognition. Foreign acknowledgment can strengthen him while attaching garrison and service conditions. Varazdat’s effective strength depends on which nobles bring followers.

[Economy and livelihood] Duin and the Ararat plain provide grain, animals, estates and mountain exchange. Nakharar houses control resources and manpower, making levies negotiated; garrisons add transport burdens along roads. Aristocratic estates support both cavalry and local life. Adding a royal contingent may remove guards and cultivators from one district. Concentration at Duin needs continued transport, while pass access affects estates’ markets and security in return. Military demands and property therefore cannot be treated as separate pools of resources with no consequences for one another.

[Forces and mobilization] Noble cavalry relies on estates, horses and followers. Pass guards require valley food; prolonged campaigning strains both defended estates and fighters’ households. Houses differ in assembly and endurance, with seasons making delayed aid hard to replace.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Both Rome and Persia watch Armenia, while Lazican friendship preserves another contact route. Roman or Persian recognition still leaves nobles asking who supplies garrisons and collection. Dependence on one protector can reduce other options. Retaining envoys, churchmen and family intermediaries separates disputes and avoids converting every disagreement into general confrontation, while keeping assistance bounded by what highland districts can actually sustain.

[Internal society] Court, nakharar houses and church have separate supporters and resources. Military cooperation does not erase local noble power. Family rivalry affects willingness to bring followers, and the three do not agree on every appointment or levy. Defined aims and duration help outside assistance become shared security rather than another contest among local powers.
arran_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Eastern Caucasian routes link Kura and Caspian directions, with different guards at narrow passages. Coastal and central mountain disputes cannot all be settled by one promise. Gabala’s valleys, uplands and Caspian approaches differ in terrain, often requiring new animals or guides.

[Authority and government] Royal standing and Persian connections both matter. Aid strengthens authority but may add levies or garrisons; subjects judge protection of land and routes. Vachagan II’s patronage works through local elites. Persian friendship adds support without erasing demands from communities of different language and belief.

[Economy and livelihood] Gabala, Kura farming and upland herding produce different resources. Grain and pass exchange complement one another; unequal transport levies cause local resentment. Kura grain reaches passes through several links, while upland animals may be exchanged in valleys for goods. Interdependence does not create equal levy capacity. Without road and seasonal knowledge, the court risks treating resources available on paper as deliveries already received. Local reports and transport arrangements consequently matter as much as the order to collect.

[Forces and mobilization] Valley assembly must feed pass guards. Maskut war strains warnings and exits; too many forces in one narrow road restrict supply and retreat. Pass and valley guards depend on one another. Food stalled below cannot sustain even a strong position; riders accelerate messages but heavy loads and families follow narrow-road speeds.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] War with Maskut threatens eastern links; friendly Persia offers negotiation and aid. Maskut war concerns land and continuing use of coastal and mountain routes. Persian support improves deterrence without replacing consent at individual passages. A great-power relationship cannot substitute for cooperation by each guard and carrier, and may require the court to balance external expectations against the limits of its own partners.

[Internal society] Vachagan II joins communities of different languages and beliefs. Mountain chiefs, valley elites and court differ over service; cooperation rests on practical patronage. Language and belief do not automatically divide communities into hostile blocs. Burdens, patronage and safety also change positions. Visible protection across regions helps Vachagan II sustain supplies, whereas indiscriminate extra demands can alienate otherwise neutral groups. The practical distribution of assistance is part of royal integration, not merely an aftermath of victory.
bosporan_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Kerch links Black Sea and Azov. Both shores need crossings, anchorages and hinterland roads; vessels cannot replace every land food route. Ships bypass some land obstacles only with weather, docks and new supplies.

[Authority and government] Sauromates V’s kingship connects towns and steppe. Titles and tradition require markets, arbitration and credible agreements.

[Economy and livelihood] Panticapaeum and strait ports rely on grain, fish and land-sea exchange. Stores connect hinterland produce to vessels; either blocked shipping or roads hurts civilians and guards. Port grain depends on farmers, carriers and storage. Delayed cargo affects debts, purchases and subsequent deliveries. Civilians and guards compete for the same food during shortage, so protecting credit also supports military capability rather than merely private merchant interests. A court can defend walls yet lose the cooperation that keeps the town provisioned.

[Forces and mobilization] Walls, docks, stores and local warnings depend on one another. Sailing escorts still need guards at home; Alan and Greuthungian wars divide land and maritime resources. Pursuing riders with every force leaves cargo exposed.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Wars with Alans and Greuthungi divide attention; eastern Roman friendship preserves maritime contact. Truces with mounted neighbors address captives and passage and can restore exchanges of animals and grain. Eastern Roman contact offers a maritime interface without guaranteed aid against every storm or road closure. Ports therefore need their own reserves and negotiators, with agreements specifying what each party can actually provide.

[Internal society] Court, Greek urban elites, grain suppliers and mounted partners have different interests. Credit requires confidence that cargo and people can arrive safely. Sauromates V risks losing supply if urban security is purchased through burdens concentrated on the hinterland. Favoring land partners alone can equally damage maritime credit. Kingship must make both see a common interest, distributing protection across the connected system rather than securing one side while leaving the other to bear the costs.
burgundian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Woodland roads and crossings connect settlements with western partners. Lombard war strains passage and return; Roman markets and envoys offer another connection. Ascaucalis links outward through settlements, woodland and crossings, requiring consent from more than one leader. An open outward road need not remain safe on return.

[Authority and government] Standing comes from success, reliability and distribution. Roman friendship strengthens bargaining without making every chief accept the same service promise. Gebicca needs kin and local chiefs to accept his summons. Royal reputation encourages cooperation without provisioning everyone or absorbing household losses.

[Economy and livelihood] Farming, animals, woodland goods and exchange around Ascaucalis sustain households. Levies remove cultivators and herders; prizes cannot indefinitely replace grain losses. Prizes distributed to chiefs must become food, tools and usable animals. Supplier losses often appear away from battle and only at the next harvest, giving common mobilization delayed costs. A coalition cannot judge the entire return solely by goods brought back by fighters; its next assembly depends on households still able to produce.

[Forces and mobilization] Followers gather along woods and rivers. Food and return dates set endurance; a route home matters to morale as much as another forward site. Woodland and river warnings reduce surprise, but expeditions still need guides, food and return dates. Long concentration reduces household capacity for another action.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Lombards are the current enemy, and western Roman friendship offers markets and diplomatic room. Roman friendship improves Gebicca’s leverage with neighbors, but Rome retains its own aims. Bounded service, passage and markets need explicit terms rather than an assumption that one operation transfers every subsequent dispute to the same partner. Agreements work through actual contributors whose resources and willingness can change.

[Internal society] Gebicca coordinates kin chiefs, whose followers still answer for their settlements. Groups set different terms on passage, reward and neighbors. Royal and other chiefs may compete for standing while cooperating to preserve settlements. Food contributions, early protection and recovered relatives shape judgments about fairness. Only continued delivery turns one joint action into a relationship usable again. Consultation therefore concerns not just ceremonial recognition but how costs and relief reach different families.
caledonian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Northern valleys, wetlands and firths separate and connect settlements. Knowledge of tracks and tides determines safe travel; Roman roads and posts form another network to the south. Roads between Alata and valleys do not everywhere carry heavy loads easily. Guides shorten journeys while animals and harvest move more slowly; firths offer routes conditional on weather.

[Authority and government] High kingship depends on recognition, gifts and protection. Roman wealth can increase standing, but lost households bring demands for an account. Gartnait’s summons becomes manpower through regional chiefs. Prestige does not remove negotiation or the need to guard one’s own fields while helping others.

[Economy and livelihood] Valley farming, livestock, fishing and exchange around Alata sustain households. Silver and prizes buy goods but cannot replace harvest; absence reduces winter stores and animal care. Valley and firth resources cannot all move with an expedition: harvests, herds and vessels have different schedules. Even a familiar bay still requires hosts and food, while returning raiders cannot assume every neighboring shore remains open. Local knowledge supplies possibilities, not unlimited access.

[Forces and mobilization] Hills and wetlands favor dispersed movement; sailing needs wind, tides and landings. Roman war requires warnings, food and routes home rather than every guard marching south.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] The western empire is the current enemy. Partners need defined aims rather than exposing every household to one raid. Hostility toward Rome leaves room for markets, ransom and particular negotiations. Chiefs compare the people and goods recovered. A maritime partner commonly offers one route or operation rather than the ability to maintain every following throughout the year, so cooperation needs defined duration and supply.

[Internal society] Gartnait connects regional chiefs with different capacities for campaigns, grazing and home defence. Maritime partners cooperate while protecting their own crews and families. Gartnait retains recognition without a major victory if shared warning visibly reduces losses. Failed harvests and missing crews also belong in distribution decisions. Otherwise royal reputation becomes a burden carried by those left behind, making the next call harder to sustain despite the prestige gained by some fighters.
danish_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Island straits, peninsula and anchorages form coastal routes. Wind and tide close seemingly accessible shores; safe landing matters more than distance alone. Food, repair timber and crews must meet at landings; lacking one prevents sailing.

[Authority and government] Gifts and safe return sustain recognition. Favoring royal kin makes other partners question another shared voyage. Dan’s standing depends on actual contributors of vessels, grain or people, each with bargaining weight. Joint sailing does not make every shore freely requisitionable property.

[Economy and livelihood] Danpsted fields, herds, fish and timber sustain crews. Vessels carry cargo and fighters, so requisition affects fishing and grain; long voyages endanger harvest labor. Loss is more than fewer fighters: replacement boats and experienced crews take time, altering the next operation’s capacity even after immediate danger ends.

[Forces and mobilization] War with Geats divides people between land warnings and vessels. Repair, water and landings set endurance; lost ships also harm households. Expeditions need boat guards as well as home routes defended. Weather and damage change withdrawal options; landing does not permit indefinite residence.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] War with Geats threatens straits; Angle and Saxon friendship eases southern pressure. Contests with Geats over landings and routes can be bounded through captives and suspended attacks that restore some returns first. Friendly partners also want defined escort responsibilities rather than involvement in every coastal dispute. Negotiation thus concerns the practical use of ships and shores as much as prestige.

[Internal society] Dan needs chiefs, owners and followers. Joint voyages pool different households’ ships, food and people, while distribution disputes spread through kin. Dan’s summons needs an explanation for food suppliers, vessel owners and home guards. Different contributions are not repaid by one identical gift. Timely return and defended homes give those without valuable prizes reasons to participate again, making royal standing depend on the treatment of costs as well as success.
ere_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Constantinople’s straits, Balkan roads and Antioch connect theaters. Danube defence and eastern supply compete for forces and transport; a transfer removes another reserve. Straits and shipping join food sources to cities, with roads carrying stores onward to camps. One open link does not guarantee the whole route.

[Authority and government] Valens shares Roman imperial legitimacy with the western court. Appointments and laws uphold authority; troops expect pay, districts protection and churches a voice in bishops and belief. Shared rule leaves each court responsible for its districts, making truthful reports essential.

[Economy and livelihood] Egyptian grain and Syrian and Anatolian produce move by road and sea to cities and armies. Delayed shipping can leave cities and camps short together and affect urban prices. Full collection recorded locally is not receipt at the frontier. Reliable reports and handovers let the emperor distinguish real difficulties instead of merely demanding complete accounts, which can conceal the stage where resources disappear or stop.

[Forces and mobilization] Field armies, frontier guards, forts and transports support each other. Infantry, cavalry and siege forces need different supplies; Tanukhid and Jazygian wars cannot empty every other frontier. Forts delay opponents while mobile armies need roads, horses and carried food. Frontier and field units cannot lend strength indefinitely; guards and replacements also count.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Jazyges and Tanukhids are current enemies; the western court and Lazica are friendly. Persia and Caucasian routes still need envoys. Cooperation with the western court and Persian diplomacy reduce miscalculation without providing unlimited reinforcements. Armenian, Lazican and Arab partners have local aims. Clear residence, service and supply terms are more likely to endure than assuming common interest commits every supporter to every eastern theater.

[Internal society] Emperor, civil officials, officers, urban elites and churches have different interests. Appointments, grain and doctrine can overlap, with local cooperation determining implementation. Urban elites, bishops and officers may support the emperor on one issue while disputing another burden. Calling every objection betrayal removes negotiable distinctions. Preserving tax production and food transport also makes imperial decisions executable; authority needs information and cooperation as well as the capacity to punish.
frankish_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Bogadium connects crossings and settlements toward Toxandria. Rivers move goods while exposing expeditions to Roman guards. Rhine contact occurs at particular crossings and markets shared by cargo, envoys and warbands. Bogadium’s safety also depends on partners protecting adjoining banks.

[Authority and government] Genobaud gains recognition through protection and rewards; Roman office, gifts and settlement agreements also bring prestige. Market households resist losing access for personal glory. Genobaud negotiates with chiefs drawing support from local followers or Roman office. These channels help but prevent personal connections becoming universal commitments.

[Economy and livelihood] Lower Rhine fields, herds and crafts reach Roman exchange through markets; some households benefit from service and cross-border links. Closed markets deprive fighters and cultivators of supplies. Market returns and military standing can belong to the same family, so fighting and exchange are not separate ways of life. Lost Roman contact reduces gifts, while Alamannic war affects local fields and herds. Households reconsider support through actual losses rather than a single attitude toward an empire.

[Forces and mobilization] Warbands need food, crossings and guides. Followers cannot leave farms indefinitely, and pursuit of Alamanni across rivers may bring a response from another side. Escorts, messages and retreat sites need people left behind; vanguards do not guarantee cart safety.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Alamanni are current enemies and Saxons friendly. Roman appointments, markets and settlement agreements remain useful. Genobaud can bargain over hostages, bounded service and markets, but an individual imperial office does not commit every Frank to the same relationship. Coverage of chiefs and crossings depends on actual participants, with agreement requiring renewal when resources or leaders change.

[Internal society] Franks have different chiefs and warbands, with some serving in Rome. An office raises one family’s standing without placing every chief in one command. Rewards only for expedition members neglect ferrymen, suppliers and guards who sustain warbands. Preserved fields, restored cross-river credit and returned captives are visible political achievements without necessarily enlarging territory. Recognizing them helps make negotiated restraint intelligible to followers seeking a useful chief.
geatish_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Southern woods and farms connect to sea paths. Land and water transport must join, so access to a shore is not enough without food. Moving timber, iron and grain from woods to landings uses roads unsuitable for every heavy load. Coastal sailing solves one leg but still needs willing inland suppliers and return food.

[Authority and government] Gifts, protection and recognition sustain leadership. Maritime reputation needs home security; a returning fleet does not excuse ruined fields. Gissur’s influence runs through chiefs and sailing partners, with owners and grain suppliers making different claims. Enduring action requires these supporters as well as fighters.

[Economy and livelihood] Hrefnesholt fields, herds, timber and iron connect to coastal exchange. Inland grain and repair materials support sailing; blocked landings also trap inland goods. Transport from inland to shore makes partners of households with different assets: timber suppliers may lack vessels and owners may lack food. Excess use of labor and materials makes repair compete with the next harvest, limiting what another expedition can demand.

[Forces and mobilization] Danish war needs landing, woodland and sea warnings. Sailing concentration reduces home guards; weather and condition limit residence, with return vessels still needing protection.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Danes are the current enemy, but competition for landings and routes can have bounded aims through escort, captive and anchorage terms. Safe return is more deliverable than control of sea space that cannot be defended. Joint sailing does not promise unlimited service by every owner; neutral owners and neighboring hosts also affect access, making continued negotiation useful.

[Internal society] Gissur negotiates with chiefs, farmers and sailors. Households supplying vessels may differ from those supplying grain; rewards affect their next cooperation. Gissur distributes returns among contributors rather than only those fighting in person. Households retaining grain, animals and timber also enable royal action. Ignoring them prevents maritime prestige becoming repeated mobilization, while visible recognition helps justify another voyage after costly or uncertain results.
gepid_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Carpathian routes and rivers connect interior, plains and neighbors. Narrow roads offer defence but can congest carts and dependants. A narrow defence delays opponents while blocking one’s own carts; families and herds need more time than light followers.

[Authority and government] Land protection and fair returns support recognition. A powerful patron offers security while potentially demanding service and food. Cibidus needs chiefs to implement decisions in settlements. Related partners retain interests and ask who guards homes and supplies food and return passage.

[Economy and livelihood] Galtis grain land, livestock and pass exchange sustain settlements. Long service removes cultivators, reducing harvest and shortening further service, while closed roads interrupt replacement tools. Counting only frontline people makes Cibidus overestimate endurance. Harvests and provisioned stops behind the army are also military resources.

[Forces and mobilization] Vandal war requires crossings, passes and grain routes. Concentration reduces warnings elsewhere, and mounted and foot followers both depend on settlement supplies. Assembly against Vandals still needs observers toward the steppe. Riders, walkers, carts and messages move differently, and familiar terrain cannot support endless residence without food.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Vandals are current enemies; neutral neighbors and Roman markets may reduce costs. Vandal truce terms can concern captives, passage and defensible boundaries without resolving every rivalry at once. Roman or neighboring support also carries duration and costs. Receiving help requires comparing those obligations with food and people that local settlements can actually provide.

[Internal society] Cibidus coordinates local chiefs and settlements; related Gothic neighbors need not recognize the same authority. Promised aid depends on followers’ capacity. Chiefs must show weaker and distant villages that protection reaches them, not only that collection begins there. Restored exchange and returned people strengthen recognition. Continued production can support the next assembly better than possession of unprovisioned land, even when holding that land offers an attractive claim to standing.
greuthungian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Dnieper crossings, forest-steppe and coastal roads connect routes. Eastern pressure and Bosporan war may approach grain from different directions. Serimum’s fields, crossings and coastal roads need several partners. Eastern reports and port goods arrive through different entrances; boats and bank space matter when dependants move.

[Authority and government] Experience, tribute and deterrence create royal standing. Without protection, punishment encourages alternative partners; delivered aid weighs more than nominal submission.

[Economy and livelihood] Serimum grain, herds and Black Sea exchange support court and followers. Tribute comes from real surplus; excess collection weakens future supply. Each subordinate following rests on food households and a chief. Tribute received in name still needs safe concentration of people and goods. Simultaneous closure of crossings and port roads prevents gathering resources; punishment for delay does not necessarily repair transport.

[Forces and mobilization] Riders, foot followers, carts and dependants move at different speeds, with crossings separating columns. Split steppe and port fronts make warning and supply essential.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Wars with Huns and Bosporans divide forces. Negotiation with Alan chiefs can aid scouting and grain exchange. Alan cooperation and Bosporan negotiation can be handled separately without making every partner join one indefinite war. Escorts, grain and residence terms turn bounded help into usable assistance while leaving each chief room to explain commitments to followers who retain their own needs.

[Internal society] Ermanaric joins chiefs with their own followers. They value royal protection while defending households and land; joint war does not erase differences. Ermanaric’s prestige coexists with chiefs seeking to withdraw families or disperse herds. Such steps may protect common resources while complicating concentration. Treating these concerns as automatic betrayal risks losing groups whose cooperation could otherwise be negotiated, making royal discipline depend on distinguishing disobedience from limits.
hibernian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Anchorages, estuaries and crossings depend on wind and tide. Familiar coasts reduce navigation and water risks; roads connect inland herds to vessels. Eblana’s coast also needs inland grain and animals. Crews knowing the shore depend on land partners; tides change departure and return, so short crossings need not finish before harvest.

[Authority and government] High kingship needs protection, distribution and recognition. Hostages and ransom affect family safety; broken promises make households reconsider cooperation. Niall’s summons works through kin and local chiefs. Marriage, fosterage and gifts build links without transferring every boat and field to one leader. High standing needs renewed participation.

[Economy and livelihood] Eblana and Irish Sea households live from grain, herds, fishing and exchange. Lost vessels harm transport, fishing and kin contact as well as raids; voyage returns must offset lost farm labor. Households treat vessels, animals and fields as connected livelihoods. A lost boat prevents fishing and returning cargo together. Ransom and raid gains need reachable delivery partners, so captured value alone cannot establish whether a voyage benefited those supplying it.

[Forces and mobilization] Voyages require crews, provisions and return plans; landings still need boat guards. Roman and Votadinian wars pull limited vessels in different directions. Home anchorages, warnings and expeditions share people, with several wars straining reserves.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Wars with Rome and Votadini cannot expand without limit. Pictish cooperation needs defined responsibilities. Different hostile shores require different terms from Roman guards, Votadinian leaders and maritime partners. Restoring one section of passage can reduce repair and food burdens without waiting for universal friendship, making an envoy’s limited agreement useful to households even when broader hostility remains.

[Internal society] Niall’s following joins kin and local chiefs. Marriage, fosterage and gifts form connections without making every district inherit another leader’s feud. Chiefs answer to kin for losses and shares after joining a coalition. Recognizing home guards, repairers and relatives caring for captives makes cooperation more than short martial enthusiasm. Return and renewed production are visible parts of authority, and neglecting them can weaken the next summons despite successful fighting.
hunnic_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Atil, crossings and seasonal pasture connect riders. Open ground permits movement, but scarce water concentrates groups in competition. At rivers, animals, wagons and remounts lengthen columns; a blocked entrance affects several groups behind.

[Authority and government] Balamber attracts partners through success and gifts, incorporating their chiefs’ claims alongside riders. Allegiance does not erase household interests; returns must continue.

[Economy and livelihood] Volga–Don herds, pasture and exchange sustain camps, with grain and iron still obtained from settlers and merchants. More followers also mean more grazing and water demand. Taking too many animals leaves new partners unable to keep contributing. Preserved local exchange can sustain later action better than extracting everything once, with military expansion requiring a supportable coalition rather than only more defeated opponents.

[Forces and mobilization] Mounted archery needs horses, remounts and rest. Pursuit wears mounts out; sieges require grain and equipment, so mobility never removes supply needs. Pursuit consumes that resource, while siege and occupation impose different duties; camps cannot be left without effective guards.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Alan and Greuthungian fronts need separate assessments of crossings and forage; success on one must not exhaust the other. Chiefs may fight together without placing every dependant and remount under one command. Bounded service and visible shares let Balamber incorporate partners with less reliance on continuous threats. Such arrangements require actual returns and room for participating leaders to maintain credibility among their own followers.

[Internal society] Balamber joins different chiefs and mounted groups. New partners add forces and reward claims; one tent cannot simply command every following. Victory gives fighters standing while camps manage recovery, wounds and replacement animals. Households unable to match the vanguard are not useless: their work and protection underpin the next force. Distribution must confront that dependence, or an impressive expedition can leave less capacity for the action that follows.
jazyg_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Plains, tributaries and crossings east of the Danube link pasture with Rome. Floods or occupied crossings force riders and dependants to detour. Herds and dependants lag behind vanguards, and flood detours add forage and escort costs.

[Authority and government] Leadership depends on protection, recognition and negotiation. Dignity affects acceptable oaths while households judge pasture and hostage safety. Zizais needs mounted families and farming households to accept shared arrangements. Grievances mobilize followers without creating lasting supply; diplomatic dignity must become household security.

[Economy and livelihood] Trissum herds and Danube markets support one another. Riders need grain, iron and markets; war makes ransom and animal exchange more important. Horses support war, household movement and exchange, making prolonged requisition hardest for weaker families. Closed markets leave valuable prizes difficult to convert into needed grain. Reopened trade therefore has military significance as well as civilian benefit, restoring supplies on which the next assembly depends.

[Forces and mobilization] Cavalry movement is limited by forage, rivers and seasons; households cannot lose every good mount indefinitely. Hostility toward both Roman courts makes defined warnings and supply essential. Cross-river action needs a return and guards for families behind. Assembly consumes pasture; endurance depends on dispersed grazing, food and kin contributions.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] War with both Roman courts requires distinct frontier aims; Quadian cooperation needs defined supplies. Quadian aid needs defined river operations, provisions and captive duties; shared anger does not make every aim identical. Roman agreements preserving pasture and enforceable safety can be useful even when limited, helping households renew support rather than choose separately between resistance and seeking another protector.

[Internal society] Zizais coordinates mounted families and farming households. Roman service rewards, grievances and market needs pull groups differently. Zizais must make dignity visible through protection. Refusal of all compromise can impose costs without an end point. Which families supply animals and which receive relief affects acceptance of shared judgments; prestige alone does not ensure the same people can or will keep bearing the coalition’s burdens.
kartli_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Kura routes link east and west and Darial leads north. Seasons and local controllers affect each road; coastal contact depends on western passage. Mtskheta’s valley joins food and people; rugged passes cannot defend themselves without supply. Snow, roads and pack animals alter northern and east–west access, making stable valleys essential to guards.

[Authority and government] Dynasty, Christian links and local recognition support kingship. External acknowledgment increases standing without guaranteeing every pass chief accepts its conditions.

[Economy and livelihood] Mtskheta and Kura grain, herds and pass exchange supply the court. Mountain guards depend on valley transport, while outside garrisons add burdens. Valleys and uplands exchange different products. Transport levies concentrated on accessible places gradually unbalance cooperation. Grain existing in one district is not grain at a pass; animals, guides and seasons determine what the court can actually use, making local implementation central to effective royal resources.

[Forces and mobilization] Noble cavalry and local guards share valleys and passes. Campaigns need estates and grain; war with Lazica also affects coastal supply. Full commitment west leaves northern observation and exits short.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] War with Lazica threatens coastal links; both Rome and Persia remain negotiating partners. Lazican war interrupting coastal exchange also deprives the interior of goods. Truce can address particular tracks, captives and escorts before eliminating every political rivalry. Roman and Persian assistance likewise needs comparison through deliverable terms rather than the prestige of a patron alone.

[Internal society] Mihrdat’s court, valley nobles and mountain chiefs have different supporters. Foreign aid raises disputes about who supplies food and service. Mihrdat retains support by preserving local judgment. Aid taking every collection and residence decision from local partners can make supporters wary. The court coordinates different demands rather than assuming all protectors and nobles seek one objective, with its success measured partly by continued supplies and willingness to respond.
kushan_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Seasonal passes and valley roads direct goods, grain and cavalry. Holding one narrow route does not feed every district beyond it. Karnasa’s valley links involve passes and repeated handling. Goods reaching one market cannot automatically continue in every direction; seasons and hospitality set the speed of caravans, envoys and aid.

[Authority and government] Royal titles, coin names and local recognition support the court. Traders ask whether coins are accepted, elites whether property and jurisdiction remain protected. Coin names identify authority while daily protection makes it useful; religious patronage must also accommodate different communities.

[Economy and livelihood] Karnasa and valleys toward Kabul and Gandhara connect crops, crafts and caravans. Coin credit helps exchange, while excessive merchant seizure harms income. Coinage identifies a name and value, but acceptance still depends on safety and delivery. Repeated arbitrary seizures from estates, religious property or caravans yield immediate goods while reducing willingness to use royal credit or support rule. Fiscal gain and political support can therefore move in opposite directions.

[Forces and mobilization] Valley cavalry, escorts and settlement guards need different supply. War with both Persia and Kidara prevents equal forces on every road. Guards and cavalry require food, spare carrying animals and seasonal access, not headcounts alone. An escort reaching a pass still needs food beyond and a return.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] War with Persia and Kidara requires relief on one front rather than unlimited commitments to both. Two fronts cannot always be answered by one force, and pass seasons can make aid arrive outside its useful window. Truce, recognition or bounded tribute needs conditions allowing local government and production to continue. Otherwise the court can lose its basis through obligations even without a decisive battlefield defeat.

[Internal society] Kipunada balances landholders, traders and religious communities. Patronage draws support, while levies can drive groups to another protector. Kipunada’s patronage must offer intelligible returns to overlapping but distinct merchants, landholders and religious supporters. Scribes, coin credit and provisioned valleys let the court keep negotiating under pressure rather than retain a title without usable resources. Their preservation links daily administration with political survival.
lakhmid_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Hira’s river food and desert movement complement one another. Wells have local users and capacity limits; reaching water does not support an entire force indefinitely, making return routes essential.

[Authority and government] Recognition comes from protection, kin and powerful support. Resolving merchant disputes and paying rewards affect continued service. Imru al-Qays II joins court, kin and Persian support. Recognition improves bargaining while kin still demand rewards and protection; outside titles alone cannot sustain service.

[Economy and livelihood] Hira joins Euphrates irrigation, river markets and desert kin. Grain, herds, escort and Persian support provide income; closed markets also deny herders grain and iron. Service rewards, subsidies and market returns do not arrive together. The court must feed people and animals before promised pay appears. Passing every gap to merchants and herders makes them question whether protection benefits only a few armed followers, with reliability depending on how shortages are shared.

[Forces and mobilization] Riders, camels and escorts have different speeds and water needs. Pursuit during Salihid war can draw forces far from river food.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Salihids are current enemies; Persian service and aid agreements change the cost of war. Salihid disputes involve wells and kin contact, so captives and reopened passage reduce household costs on both sides. Persian backing improves leverage without replacing knowledge of who guards roads and provides water. An alliance becomes useful through actual people and resources, not solely the standing of its sponsor.

[Internal society] Imru al-Qays II links towns, kin and Persian patrons. Groups exchange and compete for service returns. River partners watch credit, desert partners pasture and service. Exhausting one side to support the other weakens the connecting role on which the court’s authority and income depend.
langobard_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Mesovium’s Elbe connections depend on woodland tracks and crossings. A hidden route still needs welcoming food and stops; loads and families move slower than light parties.

[Authority and government] Reputation, oaths and distribution win recognition. Religious custom connects kin, but unprotected settlements cause doubts about royal patronage. Oaths constrain joint action alongside rewards and protection; settlements retain responsibilities for land and herds.

[Economy and livelihood] Mesovium households farm, herd and exchange woodland goods. Requisitioned seed affects the next year; chiefly gifts also depend on limited surplus. Woodland households cannot deliver a harvest before it exists, and consumed seed or breeding animals take time to replace. Even without a major defeat, reduced cultivation and interrupted exchange weaken followers. A chief’s actual resources depend on what settlements can still produce, not only the number willing to appear under arms today.

[Forces and mobilization] Burgundian war needs bounded assembly and woodland warnings. Familiar terrain aids withdrawal; prolonged absence weakens supporting households. Woods support warning and contraction but distant concentration lengthens food routes. Burgundian war needs guards, escorts and return arrangements to keep followers available.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Burgundians are current enemies; neutral neighbors prevent pressure on more borders. Locally accepted passage can deliver grain more effectively than nominal possession of a distant site. Burgundian negotiations can seek a defensible boundary, captives and suspended attacks. Limited achievements need not mean abandoning protection; their value lies in restoring the conditions that let people remain and contribute.

[Internal society] Agelmund joins kin chiefs and followers. Oaths mobilize people without erasing family claims over fields, herds and rewards. Agelmund’s oaths must constrain obligations for households as well as followers. Guards, suppliers and carriers have costs too. Rewards only for nearby warriors make another assembly harder, whereas recognized contributions and a credible end to service make common action compatible with continued cultivation and family security.
lazica_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] River ports take valley goods toward Phasis, with mountain roads continuing inland through changed vessels, animals and carriers. Sea weather and pass conditions differ; holding one node does not secure the whole route.

[Authority and government] Dynasty, local recognition and foreign contact support the court. Aid balances neighbors while making ports and collection rights bargaining issues. Opsites needs ports and valley chiefs to recognize mediation. Roman ties add support while local elites implement arrangements, including who bears garrison residence.

[Economy and livelihood] Rioni crops, timber and Phasis sea exchange sustain Archaeopolis. Rivers carry interior goods coastward, while closed passes break onward supply. Every handover from Rioni to port needs reachable carriers and receivers. Late goods become unpaid debts and difficulties purchasing the next load. Protecting commercial credit also protects court income; one extraction cannot replace transport continuing to function across seasons and between partners with different responsibilities.

[Forces and mobilization] Pass guards need valley rations and port guards protect stores and handovers. Kartli war drawing every force away exposes ports and nearby land.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Kartli is the current enemy and eastern Rome friendly. Pass disputes should not sever every east–west connection. A Kartlian truce reopening one pass benefits ports and interior together. Roman assistance needs residence and provision terms rather than presumed agreement through common hostility. Local chiefs still explain to households why they bear the obligations, making consent part of practical implementation rather than merely a formal royal decision.

[Internal society] Opsites coordinates ports and valley chiefs. Merchants need continuous movement and farmers watch garrison burdens; Roman relations also need local participation. Opsites’ mediation connects coastal and valley returns. Either side repeatedly made to pay alone loses willingness to cooperate. Port guards, grain suppliers and road protectors carry different burdens along the same livelihood chain. Recognizing their dependence helps turn foreign aid and royal standing into sustained local support.
marcomannic_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Bohemian basin, woods and southern passes lead toward the Danube. Crossings aid travel, but narrow roads hinder simultaneous movement of carts and families. Casurgis basin and southern routes support farming and exchange, while woods and rivers impose different loads. Blocked narrow roads make carts, herds and dependants hard to redirect.

[Authority and government] Protection and local recognition support each other. Roman markets, gifts or bounded service add standing, but partners compare security against duties. Vannius needs continuing participation by local families. Absence of general war does not permit unlimited collection; protection, arbitration and negotiable ties also sustain recognition.

[Economy and livelihood] Casurgis grain, herds, woodland and southern exchange sustain households. Peace allows stores and tool repair, while prolonged service removes harvest and animal care. Casurgis’ ability to store food and repair tools underpins the choice of whether to fight. If peace already consumes every surplus for outside partners, settlements have little protection when attacked. Food, animals and trading credit are therefore reserves for households and leadership together, not resources with only civilian value.

[Forces and mobilization] Present neutrality leaves room for warnings along woods and rivers while households farm. Prolonged assembly can exhaust grain before courage.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Without a general war commitment, neutrality and passage can be negotiated with Rome, Quadi and other neighbors. Bounded service to Rome or neighbors needs duration and returns, with kinship unable to replace provisioning terms. Passage, markets and hostage safety can be negotiated separately. The road a partner can guarantee matters more immediately than an abstract title of protection, especially when different routes pass different authorities.

[Internal society] Vannius needs local families and settlements. Neighboring kin make negotiation easier without obliging everyone to join each feud. Vannius needs both reputation seekers and cultivators to recognize common arrangements. Neutrality still requires warnings, envoys and prepared exits. Recognizing those contributions reduces resentment when only campaigners receive attention, and preserves the practical resources that make a later military response possible without immediately exhausting household production.
maskut_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Narrow western Caspian roads and Caucasian tracks have different entrances. Coastal Derbent and inland Darial are distinct routes requiring separate guides and pasture arrangements. Gelda’s coastal narrow roads and foothills have different conditions, with water and stops not predictable from map distance.

[Authority and government] Recognition depends on pasture protection and delivered rewards. A southern court’s nominal relationship cannot replace local kin support. Sanatruk’s summons works through coastal and foothill chiefs with their own kin and pasture. Southern recognition does not secure identical service; returns and protection need explanation.

[Economy and livelihood] Gelda and foothill households depend on herds, farming exchange and travelers. Horses need grain exchange, while excessive raiding damages the next supply visit. Coastal and foothill households produce different goods, with exchange turning animals and grain into continued provision. One captured cargo cannot replace an open route. Excessive seizure from suppliers also reduces later escort returns, so short-term gain can weaken the resources on which mounted action and local patronage depend.

[Forces and mobilization] Cavalry cannot deploy freely in narrow valleys and horses still need water and grass. Albanian war strains coastal exits and household movement; guarded entrances also need exits.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] War with Arran focuses attention on the eastern Caucasus; Alan and other neighbors can negotiate passage and neutrality. Negotiations with southern or Alan partners require separate passage, residence and force size. Protection at a coastal entrance and water at an inland stop are different practical questions. Combining them under one route name overstates a partner’s reach and risks commitments that cannot be delivered to households or followers.

[Internal society] Sanatruk joins coastal and foothill chiefs. Shares of winter pasture, gifts and escort income affect common action. Winter grazing and gifts affect kin participation, especially weaker families needing reachable relief. Fighters earning recognition do not necessarily bear all guarding and movement costs. Leadership must account for those less visible contributions if a coalition is to remain useful after the immediate opportunity for prizes has passed.
quadian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Danube crossings join settlements to rear mountain roads. Roman building on disputed land heightens passage and property fears, with fields especially exposed at harvest.

[Authority and government] Gabinius was killed after a banquet by Marcellianus. Violated hospitality makes guarantees central to meetings; oaths need a form participants can trust. Anger gathers people without replacing chiefs’ duties to food, herds and dependants.

[Economy and livelihood] Laugaritium and northern Danube households depend on harvests, animals, markets and exchange. Long assembly consumes retaliation prizes; reopened markets provision farmers and fighters. Harvest destruction removes family and military grain together, while stolen animals hinder recovery. Recovered valuables do not instantly restore damaged fields. Captives, reopened markets and farmers returning to work therefore sustain resistance alongside retaliation, affecting how long the coalition can feed people after its first response.

[Forces and mobilization] Crossing guards and mountain retreat both need people. Expeditions need a return before counterattack; slower dependants and herds require early messages for dispersed movement. Narrow crossings congest, requiring capable guards and messengers rather than every experienced person in pursuit.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] The western empire is the current enemy. Coordination with Jazyges requires clear troop and captive duties. Meeting safety cannot rest solely on an inviter’s spoken promise. Reception, departure and hostage terms influence willingness to attend. Roman frontier action may also differ from higher-level diplomacy, making Viduarius distinguish which authority can deliver which guarantee rather than accept one assurance as covering every officer and route.

[Internal society] Viduarius joins angry followers and households seeking grain and herds. Jazygian cooperation also needs distinct supply and captive responsibilities. Common anger temporarily suppresses differences that continued losses reveal again. Families lose relatives, herds or time guarding homes in unequal measure. A truce needs an intelligible response to these different costs if compromise is to retain recognition. Otherwise a settlement useful to some chiefs may still leave others feeling abandoned.
sabir_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Water, crossings and permitted camps determine movement. Riders travel quickly but dependants and herds need more time to pass. A rider’s distance is not a wagon or herd’s distance; seasons change provisions along the same road.

[Authority and government] Herd protection, credible distributions and room to move sustain recognition. A powerful neighbor’s gifts may bring service beyond local capacity. Kutilzis turns kin recognition into fighting and guards rather than counting only riders before his tent. Participating households still need camp protection.

[Economy and livelihood] Norossus households depend on horses, grazing and exchange, obtaining grain and iron from partners. Concentrated herds exhaust shared pasture faster. Moving camps require trading partners to know where to deliver next. A promise from an unreachable owner is difficult to exchange for grain or iron. Herds are wealth and the means of another journey; consuming them all for immediate food removes the basis on which households can continue cooperating with a chief.

[Forces and mobilization] Horses, forage and remounts set endurance. Pursuit toward Greuthungi lengthens the return, while sieges add provisioning burdens.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Greuthungi are current enemies; envoys and merchants offer passage and warnings. Short joint action with neighbors does not automatically become permanent service. Camp guards and remount suppliers need named responsibilities. If Greuthungian war exceeds local capacity, bounded truce and reopened passage preserve the ability to negotiate again rather than sacrifice all mobility for an obligation the coalition cannot sustain.

[Internal society] Kutilzis joins mounted groups and kin chiefs retaining their own households and reward claims. Joint action also needs people left to guard camps. Kutilzis needs rewards and protection visible across kin groups. Weaker families take longer to replace breeding animals. Frontline awards alone neglect guards and suppliers; continued support requires bounded common burdens. A chief’s standing therefore depends on both immediate success and whether followers still possess a viable livelihood afterward.
salihid_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Wells link oases across desert. One blocked source can force a detour, and available water may not support every animal together. Cultivators and daily users share water, so large camps compete with local needs.

[Authority and government] Protection, kin recognition and credible rewards sustain leadership. Roman cooperation must offer followers returns rather than an outside title alone.

[Economy and livelihood] Dumatha wells and crops sustain herders, travelers and guards. Camels and horses carry goods while consuming water and grass; escort and exchange depend on open routes. Wells bind cultivators, herders and caravans to the same place, with an army’s residence changing normal access. Occupation does not create unlimited water capacity. Well guards preserve continued exchange as well as deny enemies, and their allocation of access can affect cooperation even before a military confrontation occurs.

[Forces and mobilization] Lakhmid war makes wells and routes home essential. Riders, camels and walkers move at different speeds; food and water shares affect cohesion.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Lakhmids are current enemies. Bounded Roman service and subsidy can reduce costs. Roman subsidy and service help Zokomos coordinate partners, but someone covers food and water before rewards arrive. Lakhmid negotiations over transit, captives or pasture reduce direct costs. Diplomacy therefore concerns local terms as well as choosing an imperial protector, whose support cannot replace every daily supply arrangement.

[Internal society] Zokomos joins kin and oasis users. Herders and cultivators bear campaigns differently, including who remains to guard wells. Oasis households need harvest, herders movement and followers rewards, potentially conflicting within one campaign. Safety for guards and suppliers gives those without raid prizes reasons to sustain common arrangements. Recognition depends on whether different contributions receive protection, not merely whether the chiefs can announce a favorable external alliance.
sarmatian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Water, forest-edge tracks and grain exchanges connect settlements. Open ground permits riding, while woods increase dependence on roads and warnings. Gelonus connects forest-steppe exchange, with open and wooded ground requiring different route knowledge. Riders move quickly on grass while grain, families and goods use fewer resting links.

[Authority and government] Standing depends on household protection and returns. Fighters seek respect while families judge continuing pasture and grain access. Kasagos coordinates chiefs retaining horses and kin, not a command created by common custom. Recognition requires protection without union serving only the strongest family.

[Economy and livelihood] Gelonus households rely on herds, grain and forest-steppe exchange. Mounts and armour cost resources; drought and poor harvest weaken riders and animals together. Contact between farmers and herders makes grain and animals complementary. Armour and valuable objects need exchange before becoming food. Lost breeding stock reduces the next season, so prolonged absence can weaken mounted capacity even without battlefield losses, through household production rather than immediate casualties.

[Forces and mobilization] Cavalry needs horses, long weapons and assembly; woodland pursuit limits deployment. In Antean war, burned grain settlements may leave victors hungry. Remounts, scouts and a pasture return determine endurance.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Antes are current enemies; Alan and Jazygian contacts offer intelligence and bounded help. Antean negotiations addressing exchange sites and captives can produce more deliverable returns than unlimited woodland pursuit. Alan and Jazygian aid must be defined separately. No chief can promise resources on behalf of every mounted community, and cultural affinity does not resolve who pays, guards or supplies a particular operation.

[Internal society] Kasagos joins mounted families and kin partners. Alans and Jazyges have separate leaders; aid needs defined terms rather than assumed common customs. Kasagos needs protection extending beyond the strongest groups, since lost grain and pasture affect families differently. Sharing guarding, messages and combat risk retains varied contributors. Without them, an impressive assembly can lack willing suppliers, making the coalition’s enduring strength smaller than the mounted force visible on one day.
sassanid_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Ctesiphon depends on Mesopotamian irrigation and plateau roads, with Nisibis a western interface. Canals, rivers and passes have different seasons, requiring stores and handovers across theaters.

[Authority and government] Shapur II’s titles and traditions carry standing, but nobles, priests and regional rulers convert orders into people, horses and goods. Recognition, rewards and implementation must work together.

[Economy and livelihood] Ctesiphon and Mesopotamian irrigation supply court and armies, with estates, gifts and routes linking the plateau. Canals, labor and transport sustain income; excess collection damages future provision. Mesopotamian canals and labor cannot expand output instantly by order, and transported grain must leave resources for continued cultivation. Craftsmen, carriers and estate managers turn goods into military supply together. Failure at one link can make nominal collection unusable, so administrative reach depends on maintaining the production and delivery chain.

[Forces and mobilization] Heavy cavalry, elephants, infantry and siege forces have different needs. Horses, elephant food, equipment and transport make mobilization costly; eastern wars still leave western defence to supply.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Kushans and Kidara are current enemies; Arran and Lakhmids are friendly. Rome and Caucasian courts still require diplomacy. Western treaties and frontier relations provide bargaining tools while eastern opponents may need different settlements. Recognition, bounded aid and cooperation with local rulers keep some competition governable. Direct occupation everywhere is not the only means of influence, especially when each additional commitment draws on transport and aristocratic resources already needed elsewhere.

[Internal society] Shapur II works with nobles, priests and regional rulers controlling people and resources. Military demands must become locally supplied food, horses and followers. Noble cavalry, priestly patronage and district grain are different contributions, not interchangeable displays of allegiance. Visible links between burdens and returns sustain Shapur II’s support. Unlimited extra collection can weaken the productive core that victory is meant to protect, reducing resources available for another mobilization despite an apparent increase in immediate authority.
saxon_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Estuary landings lead toward the North Sea, Gaul and Britain. Tides and safe anchorage determine access while inland food connects maritime operations. Tulifurdum estuary and coastal roads join North Sea routes, with tides and shelter determining landings. An inland food interruption leaves sailing possible but unprovisioned.

[Authority and government] Coast protection, promised shares and returned crews sustain standing. Rewards only for fighters leave owners and farmers reluctant to join again. Freawine’s recognition works through chiefs and owners accepting vessel loss and home duties. Ships also serve household purposes beyond war.

[Economy and livelihood] Tulifurdum farming, herding, fishing and estuary exchange sustain crews. Vessels and repair materials are valuable household assets; long voyages remove workers from fields and fishing. Estuary cargo depends on tides and landings, with delayed craft materials also slowing repair. Crews fight, fish and carry goods, so longer voyages reduce local replacement capacity. Captures do not automatically cover losses across every use of a vessel or compensate households for missed seasonal work.

[Forces and mobilization] Wind, water, repair and crews constrain sailing, while the Angle frontier also needs guards. Prizes cannot ensure a return without food and water.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Angles are current enemies and Danes friendly; merchants and envoys toward Gaul and Britain remain useful. Angle war and overseas contact involve different participants, allowing ransom, suspended raids and escort to be negotiated separately. Merchant and envoy channels help Freawine identify who guarantees a particular landing instead of relying only on broad descriptions of friendship or hostility. Limited agreements can remain useful amid continuing rivalry.

[Internal society] Freawine needs coastal chiefs, owners and followers. Joint sailing shares gains and losses, with households divided over land defence and voyages. Owners, home guards and kin chiefs need terms for vessel loss and household defence. Awards measured solely by raid proceeds neglect those costs. Protected return and restored livelihoods also bring recognition, allowing leadership to remain useful without enlarging each expedition or requiring every coastal partner to bear identical obligations.
scirian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Valleys and foothill routes offer rest and movement. Roads toward Carpathians and lower Danube pass different neighbors, requiring local consent. Carsidava valleys and foothills offer fields and movement, with different neighbors permitting different routes. Light followers detour more easily than household grain and animals needing stops.

[Authority and government] Authority matters while people and land remain viable. A powerful protector brings security along with troops, food and hostage demands. Roderic needs a small following to find union more useful than separate patrons. A title does not replace land, family and reachable relief, making local leadership networks essential.

[Economy and livelihood] Carsidava households depend on valley fields, animals and neighboring exchange. Grain cushions sudden conflict, but prolonged support for many followers weakens settlements. Repeated outside service drawing on Carsidava’s limited reserves encourages households to seek separate patrons. Exchange with several neighbors reduces dependence on one promise, making supply and exits political choices as well as practical requirements. A small following needs usable alternatives, not merely a strong protector named in an agreement.

[Forces and mobilization] Warnings, familiar foothills and exits preserve people. Auxiliary service needs numbers, provisions and return dates; empty land cannot feed guards. Foothill warnings and staged retreat preserve people but still need guides and food. Auxiliary service without numbers and dates can remove home guards for another war.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] There is no general war and Gepids are friendly, allowing neutral passage and captive agreements. Roderic’s auxiliary terms need numbers, duration and a return route. A protector’s power does not guarantee relief for every small settlement. Passage, captives and neutrality address particular needs and remain adjustable, unlike transferring every relationship to one neighbor whose own priorities may change during a larger war.

[Internal society] Roderic has a limited following whose households may seek separate protection. Cooperation needs safety, food and a service end point. Families choosing to remain or move consider elderly people, children, seed and animals. Preserving them may require yielding empty ground temporarily. A chief explaining how people and renewed cultivation survive can retain recognition without holding every site, since authority also rests on whether the following remains viable after the crisis.
sclavenian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Woodland and valley routes connect settlements, with wetlands and crossings changing access. Travelers depend on water levels and local tracks. Families and heavy loads need steadier roads than fighters’ shortcuts.

[Authority and government] Recognition comes from protection and shared risk. A title cannot levy hungry households indefinitely; relief and returned captives sustain trust. Perbund needs chiefs to turn warnings into messages and guards while settlements retain daily duties. Recognition yielding only levies and no relief weakens repeated participation.

[Economy and livelihood] Navarum farming, herds, woodland goods and river exchange supply daily needs. Harvest is divided among families, seed and shared guards, with unequal village surpluses. Closed routes affect tools and imports too: extra grain collection cannot solve every shortage. Continued exchange preserves the material basis of household work.

[Forces and mobilization] Woods and rivers shelter foot movement from open-ground pressure, while crossing guards and messages need people behind. Venedian war strains village exchange, aid and exits.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Venedians are current enemies and Antes friendly; merchants and envoys support captive exchange and truce. Venedian hostility still allows negotiation over captives and passage, while Antean partners need bounded aid. Perbund must know protected roads and hosting capacity instead of treating friendship as unlimited provisions. Such detail makes assistance usable and prevents promises made by leaders from becoming unmanageable household demands.

[Internal society] Perbund needs shared warnings among chiefs. Villages have different grain and manpower, making aid without supply terms a cause of resentment. Response depends on reachable protection, not only forceful speech. Distant villages, smaller stores and existing losses produce different capacities. Coordinating those differences gives recognition a practical basis, allowing common warnings and defence to continue without repeatedly placing the heaviest burden on those least able to recover.
slavic_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Rivers, woods and crossings form routes, with rain, seasons and disputes affecting boats and walkers. Shore stops also need provisions. Stops and handovers consume food, so distant exchange requires partners along the way.

[Authority and government] Protecting fields, crossings and passage supports recognition. Related neighbors also contest land; jurisdiction requires cooperation rather than names alone.

[Economy and livelihood] Oium grain, herds, woodland and river exchange sustain households. Distant goods require vessels and intermediaries rather than being freely available chiefly wealth. Oium’s river exchange joins owners, guides and food suppliers, with cargo delayed at one point affecting later purchases. Seizure increases one distribution while discouraging another visit. Leaders therefore need repeatable credit, not only goods immediately visible, since households depend on partners returning after the present opportunity or dispute has passed.

[Forces and mobilization] Woods and banks offer warning positions while assembly removes farm labor. Sclavenian war makes boats, messages and grain as important as continued fighting.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Sclaveni are current enemies; friendly Antes and Burgundians can mediate a truce.
