Sclavenian negotiations can define usable river sections, returned relatives and suspended raids. Antean or Burgundian mediation does not guarantee every term without limit. Implementation needs identifiable parties rather than a friendly label alone, particularly where routes and households are controlled by different people along the same river.

[Internal society] Lekh joins chiefs and households. Boat owners, cultivators and fighters bear different risks and disagree over gains and levies. Concentrated exchange profits with service costs borne by others encourage fragmentation. Boat guards, cultivation and messages also support fighters; recognizing that work preserves the suppliers and carriers needed for common defence.
tanukhid_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Palmyra oases and wells connect kin camps with Syrian markets, with water capacity limiting concentration. Riders arriving first must consider families, goods and animals behind.

[Authority and government] Mavia and her spouse share protection and distribution, with chiefs’ recognition sustained by actual rewards and safety. Kin union does not remove each partner’s household duties.

[Economy and livelihood] Palmyra food, pasture, wells and caravan exchange sustain kin. Service rewards and escort income matter, but water shortage stops cargo and animals together. Service pay and caravan income arrive on different schedules, leaving well-side households covering delays. Water shortage affects cooking, herds and cargo handling as well as horses, so residence capacity concerns the whole camp. Counting fighters alone overstates what the court can keep in one place and what a local host can sustain.

[Forces and mobilization] Riders and camels follow wells. Scouts assess water and exits as well as enemies; Roman war strains markets, grain and household camps together.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Eastern Rome is the current enemy and Armenia friendly. Mavia can negotiate religion, service, rewards and captives together, with terms needing acceptance by actual followers. Roman officials and local hosts may have different authority, so envoys need to establish who can deliver each guarantee. A promise without an implementer cannot make a road safe.

[Internal society] Mavia joins kin and chiefs; she and her spouse share protection and distribution duties. Merchants, herders and followers assess war costs differently. Kin groups differ in resilience, with those losing breeding and pack animals recovering more slowly. Protection reaching only fighters makes households question common action. Shared burdens support enduring standing, connecting a queen’s ability to negotiate externally with the willingness of different local contributors to keep honoring those terms.
thervingian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Woods, passes and Danube crossings connect settlements. Eastern reports and southern envoys use different roads; closure changes other access. One guarded crossing does not replace village warnings; rivers divide and exchange.

[Authority and government] Judicial standing requires recognition. Ancestral belief and household protection can conflict, and coercion does not remove food and reward disputes. Chiefs still assess benefits to their land and families.

[Economy and livelihood] Apulum fields, herds and Danube exchange feed followers. Roman markets and local stores both matter; long assembly reduces household surplus. Apulum’s markets and stores are not unlimited substitutes. Closed exchange increases dependence on finite local surplus, and excessive collection weakens the next assembly. Protected fields and restored passage are therefore part of protection, affecting both households’ willingness to serve and the actual food available to those already assembled.

[Forces and mobilization] Woods, passes and crossings offer defence choices. Fritigern war still needs eastern warnings; followers and dependants require grain, making long concentration costly. Full commitment against Fritigern weakens eastern warnings and camp protection; families move slower than fighters.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Fritigern is the current enemy and Greuthungi friendly; Roman envoys can negotiate markets and security. Earlier war and settlement experience inform Roman negotiation, but each new condition needs local assessment. Fritigern hostility and Gothic friendship do not assign every religious or kin group the same position. Agreements need actual participants rather than broad assumptions that one leader’s alignment determines every follower’s choice.

[Internal society] Athanaric joins followers through judgment and cooperation. Religion, kin and service do not always align, while chiefs assess their own safety. Judicial standing requires recognition across groups. Equating resistance to levies with rejection of common defence weakens ties. Relief, rewards and harvest recovery reaching weaker partners can retain followers more effectively than expanding punishment, while preserving the diverse household and local resources that make a coalition usable beyond one confrontation.
vandal_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Rivers, passes and settlement routes direct forces and carts. Narrow roads aid defence but can block household and animal movement. Light forces move first while livelihoods need provisioned stops.

[Authority and government] Recognition rests on land protection, distributions and people. Forcing every family away makes followers question whose livelihoods fund royal prestige. Godigisel’s recognition requires continued participation across groups; Hasding and Siling connections do not create identical consent.

[Economy and livelihood] Carrodunum households rely on food, herds, woodland and exchange. Mounts and dependants need guards; long absence makes prizes poor compensation for harvest. Animals, fields and trade goods are different household reserves, not all portable. Objectives too far away may give Godigisel standing while leaving production behind without workers. Continued force depends on connecting both, with resources lost through absence potentially harder to replace than a single haul of valuables suggests.

[Forces and mobilization] Gepid war requires routes for infantry, riders, food and dependants. Distant fighting needs return dates and exits; one promise cannot provision everyone. Infantry, riders and rear columns differ in speed. Passes, carts and returns need separate guards; concentrating against Gepids does not secure every other frontier.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Gepids are current enemies; marriage, captives and passage can secure other neighbors’ neutrality. Gepid truce can first address captives and passage without declaring every dispute permanently ended. Neighboring neutrality and service rewards also require separate terms. One chief cannot commit all kin resources to a powerful patron in advance, particularly when those groups retain different land, routes and existing responsibilities.

[Internal society] Godigisel coordinates chiefs and groups. Hasding and Siling names do not make interests identical; union also needs delivered rewards. Guards and expedition members remember risks differently, letting distributions turn short unity into dispute. Explained protection, grain and return make bounded action acceptable across groups. Leadership then rests on maintained capacity rather than endless departure, retaining both willing fighters and households capable of supporting another response if conditions change.
vesian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Danube separates banks and carries goods and envoys. Boat numbers, water levels and stopping places determine group movement. More families increase food, cookware and transport as well as headcounts.

[Authority and government] Protection, negotiation and fair returns sustain recognition. Roman aid matters, but followers need to know who supplies food and limits levies. Followers need to know promises made to outsiders; different communities cooperate while fearing indefinite loss of choice.

[Economy and livelihood] Troesmis food, boats and markets sustain camps. More dependants increase grain, cooking and transport needs together; service rewards matter when they buy real food. Carers and usable receiving banks are also needed. Subsidies or cargo existing elsewhere are not delivery. Ferrymen and carriers’ credit therefore directly affects the leader’s protection, turning apparently commercial arrangements into conditions for political recognition within the camp.

[Forces and mobilization] Riders, families and boats move differently. Crossings, food and messages need separate people; Athanaric war makes lost food weaken camps faster than lost prestige. Crossings and grain need guards; expanding war during shortage magnifies disputes, making exits as practical as victory.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Athanaric is the current enemy and Greuthungi friendly. Rome can negotiate markets, service and grain. Roman service and settlement talks require Fritigern to explain suppliers and end points to followers. Gothic partners and intermediaries assist without guaranteeing every link. Defined delivery is more usable than general patronage, allowing households to compare the proposed security with the actual duties and dependence they would accept.

[Internal society] Fritigern joins followers and religious communities. Households want safety while fearing agreements that impose indefinite service. Followers differ over belief and trust in powerful outsiders, with shortages sharpening those distinctions. Fair shares and restored markets make safety visible. Prestige alone cannot secure acceptance of promises without clear limits; continued recognition depends on whether families and fighters understand both their obligations and what protection will reach them.
votadinian_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Hills, routes toward Traprain Law and coastal landings connect interior and sea. Ridge and estuary knowledge affects warnings and deliveries. Corda’s hills, coast and Traprain routes need different guides; maritime reports may precede inland goods. Holding a ridge does not secure a landing, nor the reverse.

[Authority and government] Land protection and local judgment sustain recognition. Roman links add credit without making every outside request beyond negotiation.

[Economy and livelihood] Corda households live from farming, animals, crafts and Roman exchange. Silver and goods enter settlements, but the next food season still depends on land and herds. Hill farming and coastal exchange need different labor, with experienced people removed from both roads and fields. Royal assessment of well-being must consider production and security as well as valuable objects entering exchange.

[Forces and mobilization] Hill sites, roads and coastal warnings share people. Hibernian war makes ship reports important; distant pursuit exposes home fields. Pursuing sea raiders thins home defence; messages, protected fields and returning people reduce losses too.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Hibernians are current enemies and the western empire friendly. Roman support still requires Padern to retain local bargaining. Suspended Hibernian attacks and captive arrangements reduce household costs. Intermediaries handle particular matters without every party first sharing one political alignment, making limited agreements useful even where broader rivalry and distrust remain unresolved.

[Internal society] Padern joins hill chiefs and coastal households. Roman friendship offers support while districts retain views on garrisons, food and passage. Coast and hills face different threats, with the sequence of mobilization and relief affecting recognition. A shore repeatedly damaged and helped last finds a friendly title difficult to value. Visible responses across households make cooperation more reliable, supporting the chiefs and guards through which external friendship becomes practical protection.
wre_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Rhine, Danube, Britain and Africa have different supply networks linked by ports, crossings and roads. Storms, broken bridges and unrest become shortages elsewhere.

[Authority and government] Valentinian sustains authority through imperial legitimacy, discipline and appointments, sharing rule with the eastern court. Formal office still requires military and local cooperation.

[Economy and livelihood] Italian and African shipping, Gallic estates and urban workshops support government and war. Collected goods still need stores, vessels, animals and roads; delays strain rations and prices. Accountability must distinguish insufficient collection from interrupted transit. Repeatedly charging the same households can reduce the next yield without resolving where goods stop.

[Forces and mobilization] Field forces, frontier guards, forts and transport play different roles. A transferred army removes another reserve; multiple wars compete for recruits, grain and horses.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Picts, Hibernians, Jazyges and Quadi are current enemies, and the eastern court friendly. Frontier envoys can still negotiate truces. Valentinian’s oaths, subsidies and bounded service require knowing who can bind participants. Quadian negotiations need reception and implementation guarantees; a local officer’s act does not mean every envoy can answer for him. Defining responsibility makes agreements more credible and avoids assuming authority reaches equally across every frontier function.

[Internal society] Emperor, officers, officials, urban elites and landholders have different duties. Armies demand delivery while districts question household capacity. Officers and officials seek imperial trust while local elites watch their own duties, giving reports reasons for bias. Verification and correction, with limited indiscriminate punishment, let discipline receive information and supplies rather than apparent obedience alone. Sustained authority relies on usable knowledge as well as the power to issue another order.
xionite_kingdom:
[Geography and routes] Bukhara and Bactrian routes join water, pasture, passes and stopping places. Vanguards pass quickly while cargo and families need supplies; missing permission redirects the whole journey.

[Authority and government] Titles, coin names and protection create prestige. Acceptance of coins affects merchant credit, while chiefs judge preserved land and jurisdiction. Holding a site still needs landholders and carriers continuing work.

[Economy and livelihood] Bukhara oasis grain, herds, coin credit and Bactrian exchange sustain the court. Excess collection harms merchants and irrigation labor. Irrigation, herding and coin credit require continuing maintenance; a large temporary extraction cannot replace another season’s production. Bukhara merchants judge usable money while elites judge land and jurisdiction. Court resources depend on both continuing to cooperate, making revenue inseparable from the protection and reliability under which exchange and cultivation occur.

[Forces and mobilization] Cavalry depends on horses, forage and pass food. Persian and Kushan fronts consume different supplies; fast pursuit does not make grain and dependants equally fast. Distant advance can outrun supply; slower families and rear columns require protected routes.

[Diplomacy and frontiers] Persia and Kushans are current enemies; dividing opponents or pausing one front helps concentrate resources. Two wars may need separate truces, recognition or tribute, with pass seasons complicating simultaneous action. Kidara compares how much local government and supply each settlement preserves, not only the dignity of its title. Limited conditions that can be delivered are more valuable than impressive obligations that leave districts unable to contribute.

[Internal society] Kidara needs landholders, merchants and followers. Holding a site still requires people willing to farm, carry and supply. Followers want rewards, suppliers safety, carriers delivery and pay. Their different contributions depend on one another; monopolized returns stop another link from cooperating, while staged delivery helps sustain participation.
